description_ru: Эссе о тишине как о вымирающем природном богатстве, которое мы теряем, не замечая, и о том, как её охранять.
text:
Conservationists, those admirable people who weep over tigers and fret about wetlands, have lately overlooked an endangered resource that is disappearing faster than any rainforest. It cannot be photographed from a satellite, nor can it be reintroduced by a team of earnest volunteers in waterproof jackets. I speak of silence: not the absolute vacuum beloved of physicists, but the ordinary, textured, living quiet in which a person can hear a thought form, a leaf fall or a kettle, three rooms away, begin to sing. This commodity, which our ancestors possessed in superabundance and never thought to value, is now more difficult to find than a decent cup of tea in an airport.

The scale of the loss is documented, though seldom discussed. Acoustic ecologists, who spend their lives with microphones and an unfashionable degree of patience, report that in many regions of the world it is now impossible to travel for a quarter of an hour without hearing a human-made noise. A natural quiet of this kind, they say, was once the default condition of the planet, interrupted only by thunder, birdsong and the occasional indignant lion. Today the last truly silent places on earth can be counted on the fingers of two hands, and one of them, I am told, is already under review by a budget airline.

Meanwhile, in our cities, the din has become so continuous that we no longer perceive it, as a man who lives beside a waterfall eventually ceases to hear the water. The rumble of traffic, the whine of a distant drill, the hum of air conditioning, the leakage of music from other people's earphones and the ceaseless, throbbing bass of somebody's idea of a good time have combined into a kind of acoustic fog. The body, however, is not fooled. Studies in several countries suggest that chronic noise elevates blood pressure, disturbs sleep and impairs children's ability to learn, and the ear, unlike the eye, has no lid.

What has been lost is not merely comfort but a certain form of attention. Silence is the medium in which concentration grows, as a photograph develops in a darkroom. In a monastery, a library or a field at dawn, the mind slows to the pace of its subject, and the world, which had seemed a blur, begins to reveal its fine print. Writers have always known this. Proust lined his bedroom with cork, and Darwin built a study whose walls kept out the commotion of his large and affectionate family. The monks, who were professionals in the matter, treated silence not as the absence of speech but as a discipline, practised like an instrument.

It is peculiar that a culture so preoccupied with the commodification of everything has not yet found a way to sell silence, though the attempt is under way. Noise-cancelling headphones, which cost more than a respectable bicycle, now offer the privilege of carrying one's own private quiet into a crowded carriage. There are meditation retreats at which, for a handsome fee, one may sit in a room and say nothing, as one might do at home for free if only the neighbours would cooperate. I do not mock these ventures, having once paid handsomely myself to be told to be quiet. Their popularity demonstrates a hunger. But there is something disquieting in a society that must pay a premium for what was once the common inheritance.

This is where a distinction matters, between silence and mere quiet. Quiet is the lowering of volume; silence is a state of receptivity, a clearing in the undergrowth where one may listen, in the older sense of the word, with the whole attention. A pianist knows the difference. The rest in a score is not an omission but an event, and a performance with no rests would be a dreadful stampede. Conversation, likewise, is shaped by its pauses, and I have known intimate friends who could sit for an hour on a bench, with a thermos between them, and feel, at the end, that they had had a wonderful talk. Silence, in short, is the grammar of every other kind of expression, and a language without it is merely a noise with ambitions.

Our reluctance to be silent is, I suspect, a symptom of fear. In an experiment that has become justly famous, researchers left volunteers alone in a bare room for fifteen minutes with a single button, which delivered a mild electric shock, and discovered that a considerable proportion of them, having previously declared that they would pay money to avoid the shock, pressed the button rather than sit with their thoughts. A quarter of an hour of their own company was, for many of them, less bearable than pain. If this is not an indictment of our age, I do not know what would be.

What, then, should be done? A resource that is shared and priceless, yet owned by nobody, is the classic victim of what economists call the tragedy of the commons, and the remedies are likewise familiar: regulation, custom and conscience. Quiet zones in parks and railway carriages are a start, as are the modest regulations governing leaf blowers, which are, in my opinion, the most unforgivable of inventions. But the greater part of the work is private. One must learn to switch off the radio in the car, to leave the headphones on the shelf during a walk, to eat a meal without a screen and to tolerate the faint awkwardness that follows.

I am conscious that an essay in praise of silence is a self-undermining thing, which has presumably cost the reader some minutes of it. I shall therefore stop, with the recommendation that the reader should close the page, switch off the lamp and sit, for a short while, in whatever quiet can still be found. It will be fragile, as all precious things are, and possibly it will be ruined by a passing motorbike. But it is worth guarding, like a flame in a high wind, because once the last quiet place has been paved over, no committee on earth will be able to bring it back.

Дифтонг: начните с широкого «а» и плавно уходите к «и»; не заканчивайте резко.
Дифтонг: начинайте с ə и скользите к ʊ с округлением губ; в американском варианте звучит как «оу».

questions.question: What endangered resource does the author discuss?
What happened in the experiment with the button?
questions.answer: Many volunteers pressed it to get a shock rather than sit with their thoughts.

questions.question: What did Proust do to his bedroom?
What does the author recommend the reader do at the end?
questions.answer: Close the page and sit in quiet.
